extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, evolutionary_biologists, and educated readers of natural history
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing evidence and mechanisms of sexual selection in birds by examining sexual dimorphism, types of ornaments, display behaviours, moulting patterns, costs to survival, and inferred female choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual dimorphism in ornamentation
rubrics_metrics.description: The wonderful difference between the sexes of many birds; females obscurely coloured and destitute of ornaments whilst the males are highly decorated in many different ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: peacock, birds of paradise, humming-birds; within the same group the males differ much more from each other than do the females. Use as evidence that selection has acted differently on the sexes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Female choice as selective agent
rubrics_metrics.description: The result in many species is due to the selection by the females of the more beautiful males.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare to artificial selection (man's selection) to argue mechanism; repeated female preference explains exaggeration of male characters (e.g., humming-birds, birds of paradise).

rubrics_metrics.name: Types and structural modification of ornaments
rubrics_metrics.description: Feathers modified in various ways—filamentous or plumose barbs, bare shafts, elongated or twisted feathers, plumes forming halos or ocelli, metallic and iridescent colours, circular spots with shaded zones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific morphological forms (rackets, bare shafts, plume elongation, ocelli) and colour effects (iridescence, metallic tints) should be catalogued and compared across species (Paradisea, Argus pheasant, humming-birds).

rubrics_metrics.name: Courtship display behaviour targeted toward females
rubrics_metrics.description: Ornaments of all kinds are sedulously displayed by the males, and apparently serve to excite, attract, or fascinate the females; males often assume special attitudes and movements to show off ornaments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document specific displays (peacock tail-fanning, Argus fan and head-peeking, lateral display of pheasants, swaying and wing-turning in finches) to link ornament form with display function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornaments exhibited primarily during courtship (context-dependent display)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain feathers and patterns are hidden until the male assumes the attitude of courtship, when they are fully displayed in perfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Argus pheasant’s ball-and-socket ocelli and primary wing-feather patterns are not visible except during courtship—supports sexual, not utilitarian, function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seasonal development and moult timing of ornamental plumage
rubrics_metrics.description: Coloured plumage and certain other ornaments of adult males are either retained for life or periodically renewed during the summer and breeding-season; some species undergo a double annual moult allowing nuptial plumage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish single vs double moult species, timing of ornament acquisition/loss, and examples (ptarmigan, ruff, widow-bird, Gallus bankiva). Use moult patterns to infer selection on breeding-season appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-moult colour changes and feather-margin shedding
rubrics_metrics.description: Males may become brighter in spring either by an actual change of colour in the feathers, or by their dull-coloured deciduary margins being periodically shed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate these mechanisms (actual pigment change vs margin-shedding) when explaining seasonal brightening (examples: Pelecanus onocrotalus, certain finches).

rubrics_metrics.name: Display adaptations to maximize visual exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: Males adopt special postures and orient feathers to show the largest possible surface of ornamentation to the female (e.g., lateral/one-sided display by Gold and Amherst pheasants; oblique tail/wing positioning in Polyplectron).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record directional adjustments and coordinated wing/tail movements as adaptive modifications to increase visibility of ocelli, colours, or patterned surfaces during courtship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornament costs to survival
rubrics_metrics.description: Various ornaments have been acquired at the expense of impeded powers of flight or running, increased conspicuousness to predators, and other disadvantages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use documented costs (e.g., Argus pheasant loss of flight, widow-bird heavy flight, peacock conspicuousness) to argue that sexual selection can outweigh survival costs and to test fitness trade-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlation between ornamentation and aggressive/pugnacious behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: All male birds with rich or strongly-characterised plumage are more quarrelsome than the dull-coloured species belonging to the same groups; those with seasonal ornamentation become more pugnacious when gaily ornamented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess behavioural correlates (frequency/severity of male–male combat) alongside plumage elaboration to evaluate linked selection pressures (sexual selection vs rivalry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ritualization and instinctive uniformity of display
rubrics_metrics.description: While preening their feathers, males study how best to exhibit their beauty; actions at first intentional have become instinctive — all males of same species display in exactly the same manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for consistency of display patterns across individuals as evidence of ritualized courtship shaped by selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence from confinement and domestication
rubrics_metrics.description: Confinement, by affecting the reproductive system of males, frequently checks the development of secondary sexual characters, but has no immediate influence on other characters; domestication can alter moult patterns and ornament retention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use captive/domesticated observations (e.g., Knot in Zoological Gardens; Gallus bankiva neck-hackles retention under domestication) to infer physiological control and developmental pathways of sexual traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of ornament elaboration independent of other functions
rubrics_metrics.description: The most refined beauty (e.g., Argus pheasant’s shading and patterning) may serve as a sexual charm and for no other purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If elaborate traits are useless for protection or other survival functions and are only shown in courtship, treat them as strong evidence of sexual selection by mate choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation among closely allied species in moult and ornament patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Closely-allied species may differ in having a double or single annual moult, and in the degree and timing of ornamental feather development, indicating gradations by which traits may be gained or lost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare related taxa (e.g., honey-suckers, pipits, ptarmigan vs blackcock) to reconstruct stepwise evolutionary changes in ornament and moult strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative explanations and direct environmental effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Some seasonal plumage differences may be attributed to the direct action of different conditions of life rather than sexual selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider and evaluate non-sexual causes (e.g., wear, abrasion, direct environmental effects) when interpreting seasonal colour changes, and use multiple lines of evidence to prefer sexual-selection hypotheses.
